items.title: Real-Time Communication Patterns for System Design Interviews
items.author: Ashish Pratap Singh
items.content:
When systems need to receive updates as soon as they happen, there are four common approaches: , , , and .

They all solve a similar problem: delivering new information without waiting for the next normal request. But they do it in very different ways, and each is better suited to a different communication pattern.

In this article we’ll look at how each one works, its trade-offs, and when to use it.

I also created a on real-time communication patterns with visuals and animations.

Subscribe for more such videos!

Traditional HTTP is client-driven. The client sends a request, and the server responds. The server does not send anything unless the client asks first.

So if the client wants fresh data, one simple option is to the server every few seconds:

That works when updates are infrequent, or when a small delay is acceptable.

But real-time applications are different. Updates can happen at any moment, and the client does not know when they will arrive. That creates a trade-off:

  • , and users see delays. If a new message arrives just after a poll, the client has to wait until the next one.

  • , and you waste resources on requests that often return no new data.

Real-time systems need a more efficient way to receive updates as soon as they become available. Each of the four approaches below solve this problem in a different way.

Long Polling works on top of regular HTTP. The main difference is that the server does not always respond right away.

Suppose a client wants to know when a new message arrives. It sends a request to the server.

  • , the server responds immediately.

  • , the server does not return an empty response. It keeps the request open and waits.

When a new message arrives, the server sends it as the response. The client then immediately opens another request and waits again.

This creates an almost continuous flow of updates, even though each update still uses a separate HTTP request.

The biggest advantage of Long Polling is . It uses standard HTTP, so it works with existing browsers, proxies, and load balancers. There is no new protocol to support.

The downside is overhead.

  • Every update costs a full request. After each response, the client sends a new request with headers, authentication data, and other metadata. For a small update, that metadata can be larger than the data itself.

  • The server has to keep a request open for every waiting client. At small scale this is fine. With hundreds of thousands of clients, the cost adds up.

  • There is a gap between requests. Between one response and the next request, the client is not listening. An update that arrives in that gap is delayed, and it can be missed entirely if the server does not track what each client has already seen.

The usual fix for that last problem is a cursor. The client sends the ID of the last event it received, and the server returns everything after it before it starts waiting.

So Long Polling is simple and practical, but it is less efficient for high-frequency updates.

Server-Sent Events also use HTTP. But unlike Long Polling, the connection stays open after an update is sent.

The client opens one connection, and the server keeps sending new events over it. The client never has to create a new request after each update.

On the wire, SSE uses a simple text-based format. Each event is sent as one or more fields such as and , followed by a blank line:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream

id: 41
data: {"type": "notification", "text": "Build finished"}

id: 42
data: {"type": "notification", "text": "New comment on your PR"}

A common modern use case of SSE is streaming responses from large language models. Instead of waiting for the entire answer to be generated, the server sends chunks of the response as they become available, all over the same open connection.

This makes SSE more efficient than Long Polling for continuous server-to-client updates.

Browsers support SSE natively through the API, and it reconnects on its own if the connection drops:

const events = new EventSource('/events');

events.onmessage = (event) => {
  showNotification(JSON.parse(event.data));
};

If the server tags events with an , the browser sends the last one it saw in a header when it reconnects. The server can then resume from that point instead of starting over.

The most important thing to understand about SSE is that it only flows . The client cannot send messages back over the same connection. If it needs to send something, it makes a separate HTTP request.

That makes SSE a good fit when communication mainly flows in one direction:

  • Progress updates for long-running jobs

But what if both the client and the server need to send data to each other in real time? That is where WebSockets come in.

WebSockets are designed for persistent, two-way communication between a client and a server.

The connection usually starts as a normal HTTP request. The client asks the server to upgrade the connection to the WebSocket protocol:

GET /game HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

If the server accepts, it replies with . From then on, the connection stays open and both sides can send messages at any time.

After the upgrade, data no longer travels as HTTP requests and responses. It travels as lightweight , which carry only a few bytes of framing instead of a full set of HTTP headers.

Example: A Multiplayer Game

Suppose we are building a multiplayer game.

  1. When a player moves, their client immediately sends that update to the server.

  2. The server pushes the new position to every other player over their existing WebSocket connections.

  3. Nobody has to ask the server whether anything changed.

Because the connection is bidirectional, each client keeps sending its own actions while it receives everyone else’s in real time.

When WebSockets Make Sense

WebSockets are a natural fit when both sides need to communicate frequently, in real time, with low latency. Common examples include:

  • Other highly interactive applications, such as live trading screens

The Cost: Operational Complexity

WebSockets are powerful, but that power comes with more operational complexity.

Every connected user keeps a connection open. At scale, that can mean hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of active connections spread across many servers.

Suppose a user is connected to server A, but an event for that user is generated on server B. Server B cannot send the event directly to the client. It first needs to get that event to server A, which owns the connection.

This usually requires shared infrastructure such as a message broker or pub/sub system that lets WebSocket servers exchange events.

Connections will eventually drop. Clients need reconnection logic, servers need to detect dead connections, and deployments need a graceful way to drain existing connections before shutting a server down.

So WebSockets are a strong choice for true two-way, low-latency communication, but they are also the most operationally demanding of the four approaches to run at scale.

So far, every approach has focused on communication between a client and a server. But real-time events also happen , where one service needs to notify another when something happens.

In these cases, keeping a persistent connection open is often unnecessary. That is where come in.

Suppose your application uses a payment provider like Stripe. A customer starts a payment, but it may take several seconds, or even minutes, to complete.

Your backend could keep polling the provider to ask whether the payment has finished. But that wastes requests, and the answer is “no” most of the time.

Instead, your application gives the payment provider an , such as . When the payment succeeds, the provider sends an HTTP request to that endpoint with the payment details:

POST /webhooks/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Webhook-Signature: t=1758700000,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e7

{"id": "evt_1042", "type": "payment.succeeded", "order_id": "ord_881", "amount": 4900}

Your server receives the request, reads the event, processes it, and returns .

The key difference from SSE and WebSockets is that there is no persistent connection. When an event occurs, the sender makes a normal HTTP request to the receiver. Once the request is handled, the connection can close.

This makes Webhooks a good fit for events that happen occasionally and at unpredictable times, such as:

  • Code is pushed to a repository and CI should run

  • An email is delivered or bounces

  • A file finishes processing

Webhooks sound simple, but reliable delivery needs a few extra considerations.

Your server might be down, slow, or return an error when the webhook arrives. The sender should not assume the event was processed. Webhook providers usually retry failed deliveries, often with increasing delays between attempts.

Retries create a new problem: the same event can arrive more than once. For example, your server processes the payment, but its is lost on the way back. The provider sees a failure and sends the event again.

That means handlers should be . Record each event ID you process, and skip any event you have already seen, so a duplicate does not mark an order as paid twice or trigger a second shipment.

async function handlePaymentWebhook(event) {
  // Skip events we have already processed
  if (await processedEvents.has(event.id)) return;

  await markOrderPaid(event.order_id);
  await processedEvents.add(event.id);
}

In production, the check and the write should happen in one transaction, or behind a unique constraint on the event ID, so two copies arriving at the same time cannot both get through.

Because a webhook endpoint is exposed to the internet, anyone can try to send requests to it. Your server therefore needs a way to verify that each request actually came from the expected sender.

A common solution is . The sender and receiver share a secret key. The sender uses that secret to compute an HMAC over the request payload and includes the signature in a header.

When the webhook arrives, the receiver computes the HMAC again using the same secret and compares the two signatures. If they do not match, the request is rejected.

Many systems also include a timestamp in the signed data. This allows the receiver to reject old requests and helps protect against replay attacks, where someone captures a valid webhook and sends it again later.

If you want to go deeper into these topics like how to make Webhooks reliable or how to scale WebSockets across millions of connections, I cover them in much more detail in my resource at .

It includes visual explanations, animations, quizzes, and hands-on exercises to help you apply these concepts in real system design scenarios.

items.title: How Engineers Really Get Promoted to Senior
items.author: Ashish Pratap Singh
items.content:
Software

Over the course of his seven-year career, Apurv has earned multiple promotions. In this post, he shares the lessons, habits, and strategies that helped him grow faster and consistently move to the next level.

Most engineers eventually ask the same question: What does it really take to get promoted?

The obvious answer might seem to be submitting more code, closing more tickets, or putting in longer hours. But that’s rarely what drives long-term career growth.

The biggest shift is not doing more of the same work. It’s gradually taking on a different kind of work: solving broader problems, handling more ambiguity, taking greater ownership, and having a bigger impact. Over time, responsibilities that once felt like the next level simply become part of your normal job.

In this article, we’ll look at how your role changes as you move from entry-level to mid-level to senior engineer, and one of the most useful habits for getting there faster.

One of the clearest ways to understand promotions is to look at how expectations change at each level.

At the entry level, you are usually given tasks that have already been scoped by someone else. Your job is to understand the requirements, implement the solution correctly, test your work, and ask for help when you are missing context.

You will still make technical decisions, but you are not expected to understand the entire codebase or business domain yet. At this stage, the focus is on building that understanding while becoming someone the team can rely on to complete well-defined tasks with increasing independence.

At the mid-level, the work is no longer fully scoped for you. You are expected to take a loosely defined requirement and drive it through design, implementation, testing, and delivery.

Owning a feature end to end does not mean doing everything alone. It means you can move the work forward, figure out what you do not know, bring in the right people when needed, and stay accountable for the outcome.

During an interview at Uber, I once asked a hiring manager what they expected from an SE2, their mid-level engineering role. Their answer stuck with me:

“You should be able to deliver end-to-end features, and occasionally build entire microservices independently.”

That was one manager’s description of one role, not a universal leveling framework. But it captures the transition well: as a mid-level engineer, you are expected to take on meaningful work and deliver it with much less direction.

As you grow in your career, the scope and complexity of the work grow with you. Eventually, the projects become too large for one person to deliver alone. You need to coordinate with other engineers, align decisions, and keep the work moving in the right direction.

This is the point where the role starts to shift from simply building to leading.

A senior engineer is often responsible for driving a complex feature, a major project, or even an entire product area with the help of several other engineers. Your impact is no longer measured only by what you personally ship, but also by how effectively you help the people around you succeed.

That means setting a strong technical direction, helping others make good decisions, catching problems early, and making sure the team delivers something reliable and maintainable.

Strong senior engineers usually know their domain deeply and have sound technical judgment. One of the clearest signs is simple: when other engineers get stuck, they naturally come to you for help.

Here’s a piece of advice that goes against most people’s instincts: don’t chase a promotion before you’re ready for it.

A premature promotion can feel like a win at first, but it often puts you in a difficult position. Your title changes overnight, but your skills and experience do not. Suddenly, you’re expected to lead projects you’ve never led, make decisions you haven’t had enough practice making, and become the person others rely on while you’re still trying to find your footing.

That gap between the title and your actual readiness can quickly become stressful. It can affect your confidence, make your weaknesses more visible, and sometimes slow down the very growth the promotion was supposed to represent.

The healthiest promotions usually happen the other way around.

You start operating at the next level you officially get there. You gradually take on broader responsibilities, solve harder problems, and build the skills the next role demands. By the time the promotion arrives, it feels less like stepping into a new job and more like the title catching up with the work you are already doing.

So the goal should not be to get promoted as quickly as possible. The goal should be to become capable of operating at the next level as quickly as possible.

If you’re a mid-level engineer aiming for senior, start looking for the kind of work senior engineers handle: ambiguous problems, broader technical decisions, coordination across engineers or teams, and projects with more moving parts. Start building those muscles while you still have room to learn.

When the promotion eventually comes, it should feel like recognition of the level you’ve already reached, not a leap into a role you’re hoping to grow into afterward.

Doing strong work is only part of the equation. People also need to understand the work you are doing and the impact it is having.

This is where many good engineers get stuck. They assume their work will speak for itself. Sometimes it does, but often not clearly enough. Your manager is responsible for an entire team, so part of managing your own career is making sure your growth, ownership, and impact are visible.

The important part is you communicate it.

Simply asking, “Can I get promoted?” usually is not very effective. A promotion is rarely something your manager can hand out because you asked. They need to build a case for it, often with other managers and senior leaders, and that case needs evidence.

So instead of leading with the title, lead with the work.

Talk regularly about the responsibilities you are taking on, the harder problems you want to solve, and the areas where you want to grow. Make it clear that you are working toward the next level, then let your actions and results support that conversation.

There is another part of this that people often underestimate: you cannot demonstrate that you are ready for the next level if you are never given the opportunity to do next-level work.

Ability matters, but opportunity matters too.

If the kind of work you need to grow is not naturally coming your way, whether that is an ambiguous design problem, a cross-team project, or the chance to lead a small initiative, do not just wait for it. Ask for it.

Tell your manager that you want to take on more responsibility, and be specific about the kind of opportunity you are looking for. A good manager will usually appreciate knowing that you are ready to stretch yourself.

One habit makes performance and promotion conversations much easier: keep track of your work as you go.

Maintain a simple running document where you record the projects you delivered, difficult problems you solved, people you unblocked, decisions you influenced, and the impact your work had.

Write these things down while they are still fresh. Six months later, you will probably remember the major projects, but you may forget the smaller details, decisions, and outcomes that make your contribution much more compelling.

This helps in two important ways.

First, it gives you concrete evidence during performance and promotion discussions. Instead of saying something vague like, “I took on more ownership,” you can point to specific examples of what you owned, what changed because of your work, and what impact it had.

Second, it makes your manager’s job easier. When they need to advocate for you during a promotion cycle, much of the evidence is already organized and ready to use.

Your work summary also gives you a useful reality check. Looking back at it over time makes it easier to see whether you are consistently operating at the next level or whether there are still gaps you need to work on.

The loop is simple: ask for the right opportunities, perform well when you get them, document your impact, and keep your manager informed along the way.

Do this consistently, and eventually the promotion conversation becomes less about convincing people that you deserve the next level and more about recognizing that you are already operating there.

One of the best ways to understand the level you are aiming for is to study the people who are already operating there.

Pay attention to how the senior engineers on your team work day to day. How do they break down an ambiguous problem? How do they decide what is not worth building? How do they explain a difficult trade-off, push back on a weak idea without creating unnecessary friction, or help unblock someone who is stuck?

Over time, you start noticing patterns.

Strong senior engineers usually have deep knowledge of the team’s domain and strong technical judgment. But just as importantly, they make the people around them more effective. They clarify problems, reduce uncertainty, share context, catch risks early, and help the team make better decisions.

That is a big part of what you are trying to learn.

Watching how experienced engineers handle these situations, then gradually applying the same approaches in your own work, is one of the fastest ways to grow into the next level.

But what if there is no senior engineer on your team?

That can actually create a valuable opportunity. If there is a gap in technical leadership, someone still needs to handle the ambiguity, make design decisions, coordinate the work, and help others move forward. Stepping into that gap can give you exactly the kind of experience you need to grow.

There is a trade-off, though.

Without a senior engineer nearby, you also lose the benefit of learning from someone more experienced every day. You have fewer examples to observe and fewer opportunities to get quick feedback on difficult decisions.

So look for that mentorship elsewhere.

Find a strong senior engineer on another team, a former colleague, or someone in your broader network who is willing to share their perspective. Ask how they would approach difficult situations, get feedback on your decisions, and learn from the mistakes they have already made.

That way, you get the best of both worlds: the opportunity to step into a bigger role yourself, while still having someone experienced to learn from along the way.

It is about gradually taking on more scope, handling more ambiguity, and owning more responsibility.

Start by understanding what the next level actually expects. If your company has a leveling guide, compare your current role with the next one and identify the biggest gaps.

Then talk to your manager about finding a project where you can practice those responsibilities. Be clear about what you will own, what success looks like, and who can give you feedback along the way.

Once the project is over, reflect on how it went. Write down what worked, but also where you struggled or needed help. Those moments often reveal the most useful areas to focus on next.

Then repeat the process with slightly more scope and responsibility each time.

There is no guaranteed fast track to becoming a senior engineer. Your timeline will also depend on project opportunities, manager support, business priorities, and your company’s promotion process.

What you can control is whether you understand what the next level requires, seek out work that helps you grow into it, learn from people who already operate at that level, and keep an honest record of your progress.

Thanks for reading AlgoMaster Newsletter! This post is public so feel free to share it.

items.title: How Load Balancers Actually Distribute Traffic
items.author: Ashish Pratap Singh
items.content:
When your application runs on multiple servers, you need a way to distribute incoming requests across them. That’s where a load balancer comes in.

But how does the load balancer decide which server should handle the next request?

It uses a .

In this article, we’ll cover the 8 load balancing algorithms you’ll commonly see in real-world systems, and the ones you should know for system design interviews.

Let’s start with the simplest one.

Subscribe for more such videos!

Suppose we have three servers: A, B, and C. With round robin, the load balancer sends requests to them one after another in a loop. The first request goes to A, the second to B, the third to C, the fourth back to A, and so on.

The load balancer only needs a pointer to the next server in the list, which it advances after every request.

servers = [A, B, C]
next = 0

on request:
    server = servers[next]
    next = (next + 1) % len(servers)
    forward request to server

The biggest advantage of round robin is its simplicity. The load balancer doesn’t need to track how busy each server is. It only needs to know which servers are healthy, so it can skip the ones that fail their health checks.

That’s why round robin is the default in many load balancers, including NGINX and HAProxy. For a fleet of identical servers handling short, similar requests, it’s usually good enough.

Round robin assumes all servers are equally capable. In real systems, that’s not always true.

For example, Server A might have sixteen CPU cores while Server B has only four. Round robin would still send both servers the same amount of traffic, even though Server A can handle far more. Server B fills up while Server A sits half idle.

To account for differences in server capacity, we can consider the next algorithm.

Weighted round robin works like regular round robin, except each server is assigned a based on its capacity, such as CPU, memory, or overall processing power. The load balancer distributes requests in proportion to those weights.

Suppose the weights are A = 4, B = 2, and C = 1. Out of every seven requests, four go to A, two go to B, and one goes to C.

Here, Server A receives roughly four times as much traffic as Server C, which matches the difference in their capacity.

Weighted round robin considers how much traffic each server receive, not how busy that server actually right now.

Say Server A receives a few slow, long-running requests and becomes heavily loaded. Weighted round robin doesn’t know that. It keeps sending A four out of every seven requests, simply because of its assigned weight.

To handle this better, the load balancer needs to look at what’s happening on the servers. The simplest signal is the number of active connections each server is handling.

With least connections, the load balancer keeps track of how many active connections each server is currently handling. The next request is sent to the server with the fewest active connections.

Server B has 3 active connections, the fewest of the three, so the new request goes to B. When a connection closes, the load balancer decrements that server’s count.

This works well when requests or connections can last for very different amounts of time.

Take WebSockets. One connection might stay open for a few seconds while another stays active for several minutes or hours. Round robin would keep handing new connections to a server that’s already holding hundreds of long-lived ones. Least connections adapts by sending new requests only to servers handling fewer connections.

The same applies to any workload with a wide spread of request durations: file uploads, streaming responses, long-polling, or API calls that sometimes take seconds and sometimes take milliseconds.

Connection counts ignore server capacity. Five connections on a small server might be more demanding than ten connections on a much more powerful one. Least connections only sees five versus ten, so it sends the next request to the small server, which is the one that’s already struggling.

So the next algorithm combines connection count with server capacity.

Weighted least connections considers two things at the same time: how busy a server is and how much capacity it has.

Each server gets a weight, just like in weighted round robin. The load balancer then compares servers by the ratio of active connections to weight, and picks the server with the lowest ratio.

on request:
    best = server with minimum (active_connections / weight)
    forward request to best

If Server A is twice as powerful as Server B, it should be able to handle twice as many active connections before we consider it equally loaded.

Server A has more raw connections (10 versus 6), but relative to its capacity it’s less loaded, so it gets the request.

Connection count is still only an approximation of actual load. Two connections can consume very different amounts of resources. One might be mostly idle, waiting on the client. Another might be running an expensive computation or a heavy database query.

A server with three idle connections and a server with three heavy ones look identical to any connection-based algorithm. So instead of looking only at connections, we can measure how quickly each server is actually responding.

With least response time, the load balancer looks at how quickly each server is responding, and routes new requests toward the servers that are responding fastest.

The load balancer measures response time for the requests it forwards, usually as a moving average over a recent window. Many implementations combine this with the active connection count, so a fast server that’s also lightly loaded ranks highest.

Here, Server A is currently responding the fastest, so it becomes a strong candidate for the next request. The goal is simple: route more traffic toward servers that are performing well right now.

This makes the algorithm more adaptive than round robin or least connections. If a server slows down due to high CPU usage, a garbage collection pause, or a noisy neighbour on the same host, its response times climb. The load balancer notices and temporarily sends it less traffic. When the server recovers, its response times drop and traffic returns.

This flexibility comes with extra complexity. The load balancer has to continuously measure and update server performance, and those measurements can become outdated quickly. This can cause traffic to oscillate between servers.

At very large scale, tracking a fresh, accurate number for every server in the fleet gets expensive. So large systems often use a simpler approach.

With Power of Two Choices, the load balancer doesn’t try to find the least-loaded server across the entire fleet. It randomly picks two servers, compares their current load, and sends the request to the less busy one.

The load balancer sampled servers 2 and 4 at random. Server 4 has fewer active connections, so it wins. The other four servers weren’t examined at all.

on request:
    s1 = random server
    s2 = random server (different from s1)
    forward request to whichever of s1, s2 has lower load

This becomes especially useful at large scale. Suppose you have thousands of backend servers. Finding the least-loaded server across the entire fleet for every request would require a lot of coordination and constantly updated load information for every server.

With Power of Two Choices, each load balancer checks just two servers, and the fleet still ends up with a very good distribution of traffic.

All the algorithms we’ve covered so far assume that any request can go to any healthy server. Sometimes that’s not what we want. We may want requests from the same client to consistently reach the same server.

With IP Hash, the load balancer uses the client’s IP address to decide which server should handle the request. In the simplest version, it hashes the client’s IP address and takes the result modulo the number of servers. That gives the server index.

on request:
    index = hash(client_ip) % number_of_servers
    forward request to servers[index]

The hash of this client’s address is 2471. Modulo three, that’s 1, so every request from this client lands on Server B. So long as the same client keeps sending requests from the same IP address, those requests will usually go to the same server.

This is useful when you want , also called .

Suppose a user logs in and some session data is stored locally on Server B, in memory or on local disk. With IP Hash, future requests from that user keep going back to Server B, so the server can reuse that local session data. Without stickiness, the next request might land on Server A, which has never heard of this user and forces a fresh login.

Suppose we have four servers and calculate . Now we add a fifth server, and the calculation changes to .

Most of the clients now map to a different server. In general, changing the modulus from N to N+1 remaps roughly N/(N+1) of all keys, so with four servers about 80% of clients move.

That means most sessions break at once. It can be especially painful for distributed caches or stateful systems, where we want mappings to remain stable as servers are added or removed.

To solve that problem, we can use consistent hashing.

With consistent hashing, we still use hashing to decide where requests should go, but we avoid the biggest problem of remapping with simple modulo hashing.

The idea is to place both servers and keys on a logical . Each server is hashed onto a position on the ring. When a request comes in, we hash its key (the client IP, a user ID, a cache key), place that key on the ring, and then walk clockwise to the next server on the ring. That server owns the key.

Here is what the ring looks like with three servers and a handful of keys. Each key belongs to the first server it meets walking clockwise.

Keys 42 and 60 walk clockwise and hit Server B first, so B owns them. Key 150 lands on C. Key 340 wraps around the end of the ring and lands on A.

What happens when the server list changes

When the server list changes, only the keys near the affected server need to move.

Add a new Server D at position 200. It takes over the keys between B (90) and 200, which used to belong to C. Every other key stays exactly where it was. Remove Server B, and only B’s keys move, to the next server clockwise. Nothing else on the ring notices.

Compare that with modulo hashing, where adding one server remapped around 80% of the keys. With consistent hashing, adding one server to N remaps about 1/(N+1) of the keys, the minimum possible.

That makes consistent hashing especially useful for systems like distributed caches, databases, and storage systems, where moving too many keys at once can be expensive. Memcached clients, Amazon’s DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, and most CDNs rely on some form of it.

There is one more practical detail. If each physical server appears only once on the ring, the distribution can become uneven. Three servers hashed to random positions might end up owning 25%, 17%, and 58% of the ring. The unlucky server takes more than half the traffic.

So real systems use . Instead of placing each server on the ring once, we place it at many different positions, say 100 or more, each under a different hash such as , , and so on.

  • or weighted round robin if your requests are short and similar. Most stateless web APIs never need more.

  • Switch to least connections (weighted if the hardware differs) when connections are long-lived or request durations vary a lot.

  • when the fleet is large or when several load balancers share the same backends. It avoids the herd effect of everyone chasing the same “least loaded” server.

  • Reach for IP Hash or consistent hashing only when requests genuinely need to land on a specific server. If you can move session state into a shared store like Redis, do that instead, and keep the freedom to send any request anywhere.

  • Prefer consistent hashing over plain IP Hash whenever the server list changes with any regularity, which in an autoscaled environment is always.

A load balancer may seem like a small part of the system, but it has a big impact on how the system behaves under heavy traffic.

The key is understanding what each algorithm pays attention to, what it ignores, and when those trade-offs matter.

If you found it valuable, hit a like ❤️ and consider subscribing for more such content every week.

If you have any questions/suggestions, feel free to leave a comment
